nameStory: Golden currant gets its sunny name from its cheerful yellow flowers that bloom in spring, creating golden clusters along the stems. It's also called clove currant because the flowers release a sweet, spicy fragrance reminiscent of cloves when you get close enough for a sniff.
description: Golden currant is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall with an upright, somewhat spreading form. In spring, it produces drooping clusters of bright yellow, tubular flowers that fill the air with a sweet, spicy scent. The shrub has smooth, three-lobed leaves and eventually develops small berries that can range from yellow to red to nearly black. This western North American native is quite rare in New England, with only a few documented sightings.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow tubular flowers hang in drooping clusters of 5-15 blooms, releasing a sweet, clove-like fragrance that you can smell from several feet away

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, bright green leaves are deeply three-lobed with rounded tips, feeling soft and flexible between your fingers with no prickles or thorns on the stems

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small round berries about 1/4 inch across that start yellow and ripen to red, orange, or purplish-black, often with a waxy feel to the skin

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright shrub 3-6 feet tall with smooth, thornless stems that arch gracefully outward, lacking the spines typical of many gooseberries

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older branches develop gray-brown bark that peels in thin strips

habitat: Golden currant is extremely rare in New England, typically found in cultivated gardens, old homesteads, or escaped near human settlements rather than in wild habitats. When it does appear in natural settings, it prefers well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations. In its native western range, it grows along streams and in mountain valleys, but New England sightings are likely from planted specimens that have naturalized.

seasonality.spring: The show-stopping season with clusters of fragrant golden-yellow flowers appearing in April to May, often before the leaves are fully expanded. The sweet, spicy scent is strongest on warm, still days.
seasonality.summer: Three-lobed leaves are fully green and smooth, while small berries develop and gradually change color from yellow through red to dark purple or black by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before dropping, and any remaining ripe berries become more noticeable against the bare stems. The smooth, thornless branches become more visible.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show reddish-brown to gray bark, and the upright, arching growth pattern is clearly visible. Buds are small and closely pressed to the stems.

funFact: Golden currant flowers are like nature's potpourri – their clove-like fragrance is so strong that early settlers and Native Americans would sometimes dry the flowers to use as a natural air freshener and flavoring agent for teas and foods.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other currants, but golden currant's bright yellow flowers and sweet clove scent set it apart from the small greenish flowers of most other Ribes species. Remember: if it smells like baking spices and glows golden yellow, you've likely found the rare golden currant.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a currant, golden currant berries are quite different from the dried currants you find in baking, which are actually tiny raisins made from grapes. True currants like this one belong to an entirely different plant family and have their own unique tart-sweet flavor.
compareHints: Golden currant stands out among New England's Ribes species with its bright yellow flowers and sweet fragrance, while most relatives like skunk currant and American black currant have small, greenish or whitish flowers. Unlike prickly gooseberry and other spiny relatives, golden currant has completely smooth, thornless stems. Its three-lobed leaves are also smoother and less deeply cut than those of swamp currant.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's currants and gooseberries, skunk currant is unique for its strong musky odor and preference for cooler, northern forests.
Among New England's Ribes species, prickly gooseberry is the most heavily armed with spines, making it easy to distinguish from the spineless currants like red currant or American black currant.
Unlike its gooseberry relatives in the Ribes genus, red currant has completely smooth, thornless stems and bears its fruit in long drooping clusters rather than scattered individual berries.
Among New England's Ribes species, swamp currant stands out for its incredibly dense coat of small prickles - no other currant or gooseberry in the region is quite so thoroughly armored.

Among its Ribes relatives, smooth gooseberry is distinguished by having fewer thorns than prickly gooseberry but more than the currants, and its berries grow individually rather than in the long clusters typical of red and black currants.
Among New England's Ribes species, American black currant is distinguished by its strong musky leaf scent and completely smooth stems.
Unlike its spiny gooseberry relatives in the Ribes family, northern redcurrant is completely thornless and has a sprawling rather than upright growth habit.
European gooseberry has much more prominent three-pronged spines than our native prickly gooseberry or smooth gooseberry.
Appalachian gooseberry stands out from other Ribes species by its sweet berries and relatively smooth stems - unlike the very thorny prickly gooseberry or the skunky-smelling skunk currant.
Among the Ribes family, blackcurrant stands out for lacking thorns (unlike most gooseberries) and having that distinctive strong musky leaf scent.
